extracted.intended_audience: district court judges, patent litigators, and counsel in §101 patent eligibility litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Assess whether asserted patent claims are directed to patent‑ineligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. §101 using the two-step Alice/Mayo framework, and decide Rule 12(c) motions where appropriate. This covers evaluating claim specificity, inventive concept, and whether claims improve computer functionality or merely recite generic techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion for judgment on the pleadings standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion for judgment on the pleadings should be granted if the movant establishes that there are no material issues of fact, and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In considering such a motion, a court must accept all of the allegations in the pleadings of the party against whom the motion is addressed as true and draw all reasonable inferences in favor of the non-moving party. (Int'l Bus. Machines v. Groupon; Zimmerman v. Corbett.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory scope of §101
rubrics_metrics.description: "Whoever invents or discovers any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof, may obtain a patent therefor, subject to the conditions and requirements of this title." 35 U.S.C. §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the baseline definition of patent-eligible subject matter; judicially-created exceptions limit this statutory scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial exceptions to §101
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas are not patentable subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exceptions exist because monopolization of basic tools of scientific and technological work 'might tend to impede innovation' (Alice). Abstract ideas include mathematical formulas and calculations (Gottschalk v. Benson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo two-step framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1: Determine whether the claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea). Step 2: If so, consider the elements of each claim individually and as an ordered combination to determine whether there is an "inventive concept" sufficient to ensure the patent amounts to significantly more than the ineligible concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two steps are related and involve overlapping scrutiny of claim content. (Alice; Mayo; Elec. Power Grp.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of validity and evidentiary burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Issued patents are presumed valid, but this presumption is rebuttable; a party challenging validity must show underlying facts by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Microsoft Corp. v. i4i Ltd. Partnership; factual attacks governed by Berkheimer where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step-one inquiry for computer-technology claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask whether the claims focus on a specific means or method that improves the relevant technology or are instead directed to a result or effect that itself is the abstract idea and merely invoke generic processes and machinery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that simply claim a result or effect (e.g., content transfer) using generic components are more likely abstract. (McRO; Ancora; Universal Secure Registry.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract-idea examples relevant to access/authentication claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts such as content transfer based on meeting a condition, providing information based on user/location/condition, and controlling access to resources are abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited examples: 'content transfer, even if based on meeting a condition, is an abstract idea' (Sanderling Mgmt. v. Snap); 'customizing information based on information known about the user' (Intelli. Ventures); 'controlling access to resources' analogous to library/card-holding members, building floor access, or loan decisions (Ericsson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of claim/specification specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims/specification must describe how the elements recited in the claims refer to technological features functioning together to improve technology in a specific way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A general recitation of processors/instructions/devices or placement in generic devices without explanation of how they effect a technical improvement is insufficient. (Packet Intel. LLC v. NetScout.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventional components and standards are not inventive
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of well-known methods, conventional computer components, and established standards (e.g., XOR operations, ISO protocols) does not by itself provide an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent disclosure that only incorporates known techniques or standards without describing a nonconventional application will likely fail §101. The opinion cites patent passages describing spread spectrum signals, XOR, and ISO standards as conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence or ordering of conventional steps alone is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that merely requires a specific ordering of transmissions/receipts or a sequence of conventional authentication steps, without explaining how that ordering is a nonconventional technical solution, does not supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Result-oriented claims that do not provide limiting detail confining the claim to a particular solution are abstract. Compare Affinity Labs (abstract) to Bascom (specific location of filtering tool as inventive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice step-two — inventive concept must be 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: At step two, courts examine whether elements individually and as an ordered combination add an inventive concept that transforms the abstract idea into a patent-eligible application; mere use of a generic computer performing generic functions is not enough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying a computer to perform conventional tasks does not satisfy step two (Alice; Mayo; Prism Techs.). The inquiry looks for a specific technical solution or improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: What counts as a sufficient inventive concept (exemplar features)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that identify specific technical solutions or improvements — e.g., varying how check data is generated by modifying permutations, storing records in particular modifiable non-volatile memory for verification, object-oriented key managers, adding data fields to reduce latency, or hardware-based RFID serial-number data structures — have been found to supply inventive concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited favorable examples: Koninklijke KPN (modifying permutation), Ancora (storing license record in particular BIOS area), TecSec (object-oriented key manager), Uniloc (additional data field to reduce latency), Adasa (hardware-based RFID structure). These demonstrate the specificity required to transform a claim from claiming only a result to claiming a way of achieving it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining conventional authentication techniques is not inventive
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining multiple conventional, long-standing authentication techniques in a cumulative way does not produce an inventive concept and remains directed to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Universal Secure Registry and Prism Techs illustrate that aggregating known techniques without a nonconventional departure fails §101; the court found the #564 patent analogous to those cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlap and porosity between Alice step one and step two
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinction between step one and step two can be porous; considerable overlap exists and in some cases the analysis may be accomplished without going beyond step one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that step-one specificity analysis and step-two inventive-concept inquiry can bleed into one another (Amdocs; CosmoKey concurring observations).
